passage: Today we turn to ancient Roman architecture, focusing specifically on aqueducts, one of the empire's most impressive engineering achievements. Aqueducts were structures built to transport water over long distances, often from mountain springs into cities, using nothing but gravity. Many people assume the Romans invented the aqueduct, but earlier civilisations, including the Assyrians, had already built similar water channels centuries before; what the Romans actually contributed was scale and precision, building networks stretching over four hundred kilometres in some cases. The famous arched sections, the parts most people picture, actually made up only a small portion of most aqueducts — roughly eighty percent ran underground through covered channels, which protected the water from contamination and evaporation. Engineers calculated a very gentle downward slope, often just a few centimetres per kilometre, to keep water flowing steadily without eroding the channel. Some aqueducts also included settling tanks, which allowed sediment to sink before the water continued its journey. Remarkably, several Roman aqueducts, such as the Aqua Virgo in Rome, remained partially in use for well over a thousand years, a testament to the durability of Roman engineering.
stem: What is the main topic of this lecture?
options: The fall of the Roman Empire

passage: Today's lecture examines microplastic pollution in our oceans, a growing environmental concern. Microplastics are defined as plastic fragments smaller than five millimetres, and they enter the ocean through two main pathways: the breakdown of larger plastic waste, and direct release from products like synthetic clothing fibres and cosmetic microbeads. For years, scientists believed most ocean microplastics came from the physical breakdown of large debris like bottles and bags, but more recent studies suggest that synthetic textile fibres, released every time we wash clothes, may actually account for an even larger share of ocean microplastics than previously assumed. These particles are now found in even the most remote environments on Earth, including Arctic sea ice and deep ocean trenches over ten kilometres below the surface. Marine organisms, from plankton to whales, ingest these particles, often mistaking them for food, and there is growing evidence that microplastics move up the food chain, eventually appearing in seafood consumed by humans. Some countries have responded by banning microbeads in cosmetic products, and researchers are also developing filters for washing machines to catch textile fibres before they reach wastewater systems. Still, full solutions remain years away.

passage: This lecture covers the fundamentals of volcanic activity and its role in shaping the Earth's surface. Volcanoes form where molten rock, called magma, rises through weaknesses in the Earth's crust, most commonly along tectonic plate boundaries. Many people assume that most volcanoes are found where plates are pulling apart, but in fact, the majority of the world's active volcanoes occur along convergent boundaries, particularly around the Pacific Ring of Fire, where plates are colliding and one is forced beneath another. Not all eruptions look the same: some, like Hawaii's Kilauea, produce relatively gentle flows of fluid lava, while others, like Mount St. Helens in 1980, produce violent explosive eruptions due to thicker, gas-rich magma. Scientists monitor volcanoes using several methods, including seismographs to detect underground tremors, and gas sensors to track changes in sulphur dioxide emissions, which often rise before an eruption. On average, around fifty to sixty volcanoes erupt somewhere in the world each year, though most are minor and cause little damage. Despite the risks, volcanic soil is often extremely fertile, which is why millions of people continue to live near active volcanoes worldwide.

passage: Today's lecture looks at how certain plants have evolved special adaptations to perform photosynthesis more efficiently in hot, dry environments. Most plants use what's called the C3 pathway to convert carbon dioxide and sunlight into energy, but this process becomes inefficient in high temperatures, since plants lose more water through small leaf openings called stomata. For a long time, botanists believed that C4 photosynthesis, a more water-efficient pathway, evolved only once in plant history, but genetic studies over the past fifteen years reveal that it actually evolved independently more than sixty separate times across different plant families. Crops like maize and sugarcane use this C4 pathway, which allows them to concentrate carbon dioxide inside their leaves before processing it, reducing water loss significantly. A third, even more extreme adaptation, called CAM photosynthesis, is used by desert plants like cacti; these plants open their stomata only at night, when temperatures are cooler, storing carbon dioxide until daylight, when photosynthesis actually occurs. Understanding these adaptations has become increasingly important for agricultural scientists, who are researching whether some of these water-saving traits could eventually be introduced into staple crops like wheat and rice.
stem: What is the main topic of this lecture?
options: Plant adaptations for photosynthesis in hot, dry environments

passage: This lecture explores the social behaviour of honeybee colonies, one of the most complex examples of cooperation in the animal kingdom. A single colony can contain tens of thousands of bees, all descended from one queen, and organised into distinct roles, including workers, drones, and the queen herself. One of the most fascinating behaviours is the "waggle dance," a figure-eight movement performed by worker bees to communicate the location of food sources to the rest of the colony. Researchers long assumed the dance only conveyed direction, but decoding studies conducted in the 1990s and beyond revealed that the duration of the waggle phase also communicates distance, with longer waggles indicating food sources further away. Bees can also adjust the angle of the dance relative to gravity to represent the angle relative to the sun outside the hive, an extraordinary feat of natural navigation. Beyond foraging, colonies also make collective decisions, such as choosing a new nest site when swarming, through a democratic-like process where scout bees advertise different locations and the colony gradually reaches consensus. This decision-making process can take anywhere from a few hours to several days, depending on how divided the scouts initially are.

passage: This lecture explores the social behaviour of honeybee colonies, one of the most complex examples of cooperation in the animal kingdom. A single colony can contain tens of thousands of bees, all descended from one queen, and organised into distinct roles, including workers, drones, and the queen herself. One of the most fascinating behaviours is the "waggle dance," a figure-eight movement performed by worker bees to communicate the location of food sources to the rest of the colony. Researchers long assumed the dance only conveyed direction, but decoding studies conducted in the 1990s and beyond revealed that the duration of the waggle phase also communicates distance, with longer waggles indicating food sources further away. Bees can also adjust the angle of the dance relative to gravity to represent the angle relative to the sun outside the hive, an extraordinary feat of natural navigation. Beyond foraging, colonies also make collective decisions, such as choosing a new nest site when swarming, through a democratic-like process where scout bees advertise different locations and the colony gradually reaches consensus. This decision-making process can take anywhere from a few hours to several days, depending on how divided the scouts initially are.
stem: What did researchers originally believe the waggle dance conveyed?
options: Both direction and distance from the start

passage: Today we examine the historical significance of the Silk Road, the network of trade routes connecting East Asia with the Mediterranean world. Many people picture the Silk Road as a single continuous road, but it was actually a shifting web of overland and maritime routes, used by different traders for different sections rather than any one merchant travelling the entire distance. The network is generally thought to have flourished for around fifteen hundred years, from roughly the second century BCE until the fifteenth century CE, though trade along parts of it continued long after. While silk was certainly an important commodity, giving the route its modern name, goods traded included spices, precious stones, paper, and even ideas — Buddhism, for instance, spread from India into China largely along these routes. Trade wasn't limited to physical goods, either; the Silk Road also facilitated the exchange of technologies, including papermaking techniques, which eventually reached Europe centuries after being developed in China. Cities along the route, such as Samarkand, grew wealthy as trading hubs, serving as meeting points for merchants, scholars, and travellers from vastly different cultures, making the Silk Road one of history's most influential channels of cultural exchange.

passage: This lecture traces the evolution of urban transportation planning over the past century. In the early twentieth century, cities were largely designed around pedestrians, trams, and rail, but the rapid rise of car ownership after the Second World War led planners to prioritise road building and parking, often at the expense of public transport and walkability. For decades, the dominant belief among planners was that building more roads would reduce traffic congestion, but studies conducted from the 1990s onward demonstrated a phenomenon called "induced demand," showing that expanded roads actually tend to attract more traffic over time rather than easing it. This finding gradually shifted planning philosophy, and by the early 2000s, many cities began reinvesting in public transport, cycling infrastructure, and pedestrian zones. Copenhagen, for example, transformed a car-dominated main street into a pedestrian-only zone starting in 1962, and today over sixty percent of residents commute to work or school by bicycle. Modern transportation planning now increasingly incorporates data from mobile devices to model traffic flow in real time, allowing cities to adjust traffic signals dynamically rather than relying on fixed timing, which represents a significant shift from the rigid, car-centred planning of the mid-twentieth century.

passage: Today's lecture looks at colour psychology, the study of how colours influence human emotion and behaviour, particularly in marketing contexts. It's often claimed in popular articles that specific colours produce universal emotional reactions — for instance, that blue always creates feelings of calm and red always increases appetite — but rigorous cross-cultural research suggests these effects are far less consistent than commonly assumed, and are shaped heavily by personal experience and cultural background rather than being universal. What research does support more strongly is that colour affects brand recognition — one widely cited study found that consistent colour use can increase brand recognition by up to eighty percent. Retailers also use colour strategically in store design; red is frequently used in clearance sales, partly because it draws attention quickly, while blue and green tones are common in environments meant to encourage longer browsing, such as bookstores and spas. Interestingly, the effectiveness of colour also depends heavily on context — a colour that works well on a website button might have the opposite effect if used across an entire product packaging design. Marketers today increasingly test colour choices through controlled experiments rather than relying on generalised assumptions about colour meaning.

passage: This lecture explores how organisms have adapted to survive in the deep sea, one of the most extreme environments on Earth. Below around one thousand metres, sunlight cannot penetrate at all, meaning photosynthesis is impossible, and temperatures typically hover just above freezing. For a long time, scientists assumed deep-sea ecosystems depended entirely on food sinking down from sunlit surface waters, a process known as marine snow, but the discovery of hydrothermal vent communities in the 1970s revealed an entirely different energy source: bacteria that convert chemicals released from the vents into energy through a process called chemosynthesis, supporting entire food webs independent of sunlight. Many deep-sea creatures have evolved bioluminescence, the ability to produce their own light, which they use for purposes ranging from attracting prey to confusing predators. Pressure is another major challenge — at depths of several kilometres, pressure can exceed several hundred times that at the surface, so deep-sea organisms have evolved flexible cell membranes and reduced or absent gas-filled spaces like swim bladders, which would otherwise collapse. Because of the difficulty of exploring these depths, scientists estimate that a significant proportion of deep-sea species remain completely undiscovered.

Pressure is another major challenge — at depths of several kilometres, pressure can exceed several hundred times that at the surface, so deep-sea organisms have evolved flexible cell membranes and reduced or absent gas-filled spaces like swim bladders, which would otherwise collapse. Because of the difficulty of exploring these depths, scientists estimate that a significant proportion of deep-sea species remain completely undiscovered.

options: Food sinking down from sunlit surface waters

passage: Today's final lecture in this series looks at the history of space exploration, from its earliest beginnings to the present day. The space age is generally considered to have begun in 1957 with the launch of Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, which surprised much of the world and triggered intense competition between the Soviet Union and the United States. Many people assume the Apollo 11 moon landing in 1969 was the first time humans travelled beyond Earth's orbit, but in fact, Apollo 8, launched the previous year in 1968, was the first crewed mission to leave Earth's orbit and circle the Moon, without landing. Following the Apollo programme, space exploration shifted focus toward long-duration missions, exemplified by space stations like Mir and later the International Space Station, which has been continuously occupied by rotating crews since the year 2000. In recent decades, private companies have increasingly taken on roles previously reserved for government agencies, dramatically reducing launch costs through innovations like reusable rockets. Looking ahead, current plans focus on returning humans to the Moon and eventually sending crewed missions to Mars, though most realistic timelines suggest a crewed Mars landing remains at least a decade or more away.
